title: 60 SQL Practice Queries with Answers on PostgreSQL
summary: Sixty graded SQL drills on PostgreSQL over an employees/departments/orders schema, from basic SELECTs through joins, subqueries, window functions and CTEs to classic interview scenarios. Each task has runnable solution code and the result it returns on the sample data.

chapters.title: 60 SQL Queries: Cover
points: Basics: 7 tasks on SELECT, aliases, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and LIMIT
Filtering: 7 tasks on WHERE, IN, BETWEEN, LIKE and NULL handling
Aggregates: 8 tasks on COUNT, SUM, AVG, GROUP BY and HAVING
Joins: 8 tasks on INNER, LEFT, self and anti joins
Subqueries: 7 tasks on scalar, IN, EXISTS and correlated subqueries
Window functions: 8 tasks on ranking, LAG/LEAD and running totals
CTEs: 6 tasks on WITH, chained CTEs and recursive CTEs
Interview scenarios: 9 classics such as nth highest salary and duplicates
Engine: PostgreSQL 16, every query runs as written

chapters.title: The Practice Schema and Sample Data
points: departments(dept_id, dept_name, location): 4 rows, with Engineering, Sales, HR and an empty Legal
employees(emp_id, name, dept_id, manager_id, salary, hire_date, email): 12 rows including one NULL dept_id and one NULL manager_id (the CEO)
orders(order_id, emp_id, customer, amount, order_date, status): sales orders placed by employees across 2024 and 2025
Foreign keys: employees.dept_id → departments, employees.manager_id → employees (self-reference), orders.emp_id → employees
Salary sample: Engineering 90k to 150k, Sales 60k to 95k, HR 55k to 70k, with a deliberate tie at 90000
Why the data has traps: NULLs, ties, duplicate emails and a department with no staff
How to load it: one CREATE TABLE and INSERT script, run once in psql
Conventions: lowercase snake_case, ISO dates, every result sorted so output is deterministic

chapters.title: Basics: SELECT, Aliases and Sorting
points: List all columns of every employee with SELECT *, and say why it is risky in production
Select only name and salary of every employee
Show each employee's annual salary as a column aliased annual_pay (salary * 12)
Return the distinct department ids used in employees with DISTINCT
List employees sorted by salary descending, then name ascending
Return the 5 most recently hired employees with ORDER BY hire_date DESC LIMIT 5
Skip the first 3 employees by name and return the next 4 with OFFSET, and note why OFFSET is slow on large tables

chapters.title: Filtering: WHERE, IN, LIKE and NULL
points: Find employees in department 10 earning more than 80000
Find employees whose salary is between 60000 and 90000, inclusive, with BETWEEN
Find employees in Engineering or Sales using IN (id list)
Find employees whose name starts with 'A' using LIKE 'A%'
Find employees whose email contains 'corp' regardless of case using ILIKE
Find employees with no department using IS NULL, and show why = NULL returns nothing
Find employees not in department 10 without losing the NULL-department rows (IS DISTINCT FROM)

chapters.title: Aggregates: COUNT, SUM, GROUP BY, HAVING
points: Count all employees, and compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(dept_id) when NULLs are present
Compute the total, average, minimum and maximum salary in one query
Count employees per department with GROUP BY dept_id
Find the average salary per department, rounded to 2 decimals
List departments with more than 3 employees using HAVING
Find the total order amount per employee, highest first
Count orders per status using FILTER (WHERE ...) to get shipped and cancelled counts in one row
Find the number of distinct customers per month using COUNT(DISTINCT customer) and date_trunc

chapters.title: Joins: Combining Tables
points: List each employee with their department name using INNER JOIN
List all employees including those without a department using LEFT JOIN
Find departments that have no employees using LEFT JOIN ... WHERE e.emp_id IS NULL
List every employee with their manager's name using a self join
Find employees who earn more than their manager
Show total order amount per department name by joining orders, employees and departments
Find employees who have placed no orders using an anti join
Return every department with its employee count, including Legal at 0, using LEFT JOIN and COUNT(e.emp_id)

chapters.title: Subqueries: Scalar, IN, EXISTS, Correlated
points: Find employees earning more than the company average using a scalar subquery
Find employees who work in a department located in 'Hyderabad' using IN (subquery)
Find employees who have at least one order using EXISTS
Find employees with no orders using NOT EXISTS, and say why it beats NOT IN when NULLs exist
Find employees earning above their own department's average with a correlated subquery
Find the department with the highest total salary using a subquery in HAVING
Select each employee's name next to their order count using a scalar subquery in the SELECT list

chapters.title: Window Functions: Ranking, LAG and Running Totals
points: Number all employees by salary descending with ROW_NUMBER()
Rank employees by salary with RANK() and show how the tie at 90000 leaves a gap
Rank employees by salary with DENSE_RANK() so no ranks are skipped
Rank employees within each department using PARTITION BY dept_id
Show each employee's salary next to the average salary of their department with AVG() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)
For each order, show the previous order amount for the same employee using LAG()
Compute a running total of order amount by order_date using SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ... ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
Split employees into 4 salary quartiles with NTILE(4)

chapters.title: CTEs: WITH, Chaining and Recursion
points: Rewrite the above-department-average query with a WITH clause
Compute total sales per employee in a CTE, then join it to employee names
Chain two CTEs: monthly revenue first, then the months above the average of those months
Use a CTE to find the top-selling employee in each department
Build the full management chain below the CEO using WITH RECURSIVE
Generate the numbers 1 to 10 with a recursive CTE, and show the termination condition

chapters.title: Interview Scenarios: The Classics
points: Find the 2nd highest salary using DENSE_RANK, and return NULL if it does not exist
Find the nth highest salary with a parameter-style query (n = 3) and a LIMIT/OFFSET variant
Find duplicate emails in employees using GROUP BY ... HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
Delete duplicate rows while keeping the lowest emp_id using ROW_NUMBER() or ctid
Compute the cumulative order amount per employee by month
Find the top 2 earners in every department
Find the median salary with percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP
Find missing ids in a sequence using generate_series and an anti join
Compute month-over-month revenue growth percentage using LAG()

chapters.title: SQL Drills Cheatsheet
points: Logical clause order: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups
Join picker: INNER keeps matches, LEFT keeps all left rows, anti join finds missing rows
NULL rules: use IS NULL, COUNT(col) skips NULLs, NOT IN breaks on NULLs
ROW_NUMBER vs RANK vs DENSE_RANK on ties
Frame default with ORDER BY is RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING to CURRENT ROW, so use ROWS for exact running totals
Subquery vs CTE vs join: pick for clarity, and check EXPLAIN for speed
Common mistakes: SELECT * in production, selecting a column that is not grouped, OFFSET paging on big tables
Interview patterns: nth highest, duplicates, top N per group, running totals, gaps
